title: Building Respectful Institutional Relationships
summary: Guidance for schools, museums, towns, and preservation groups building accountable relationships with Native Nations.
content:
Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

How can schools, museums, towns, and preservation groups build better relationships with local Native Nations?

Institutions must move past generic consultation toward active, reciprocal partnerships that respect tribal sovereignty. This means co-developing programs with tribal historic preservation officers, repatriating sacred objects under NAGPRA, using Native-authored curricula, and paying Native experts proper compensation.

Building respectful institutional relationships requires schools, towns, and museums to transition from paternalistic curation toward cooperative partnerships that honor Indigenous sovereignty and intellectual authority. Historically, local historical societies and state curricula have marginalized Native histories or incorrectly conflated Algonquian nations with the Iroquois (Strong 2001, pp. 115-116). To rectify this, schools should adopt Native-designed curricula, such as the Shinnecock Title V Heritage Project materials, which teach authentic histories in public contract schools (Strong 1998, pp. 50-51). Museums and researchers must actively consult with descendant communities and tribal historic preservation officers on archaeological investigations and National Register nominations, rather than treating Native artifacts as passive collectibles (McGovern 2015, pp. 10, 43). Under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) of 1990, institutions must repatriate ancestral remains and sacred objects, facilitating a consensus-driven process of return, as demonstrated by the Smithsonian's collaboration with Long Island tribal historians (Jensen 2015, pp. 84-85). Most importantly, organizations must formally credit and financially compensate Native consultants, educators, and artists for their expertise, ensuring that collaboration is mutually beneficial and respects tribal self-determination.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. 115-116.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 50-51.
  • Allison Manfra McGovern, Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montaukett (2015), pp. 10, 43.
  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation (2015), pp. 84-85.
why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
